## Methods

Synthesis of Ni17W3–WO2. 4.0 mmol of NiC4H6O4·4H2O (Macklin, 99.9%) and 4.0 mmol of Na2WO4·2H2O (Macklin, 99%) were dissolved in 200 mL of deionized water (DW), which was placed in a water bath and heated to 80 oC for 3 hours. The mixture was filtered and washed several times with DW and ethanol (Sinopharm, ≥99.7), followed by drying and further annealing at 600 oC in the air for 1 hour to obtain the NiWO4 precursor. The Ni17W3–WO2 heterostructure was produced by annealing the NiWO4 precursor at 600 oC in N2/H2 (containing 8% H2) atmosphere for 10 hours with a ramp rate of 5 oC min−1.

Synthesis of WO2. 1.0 g of (NH4)6H2W12O40·xH2O (Macklin, 99.5%) was spread in a ceramic boat, which was placed in a tube furnace and heated to 700 oC in an air atmosphere for 1 hour with a ramp rate of 5 oC min−1. The product was then annealed at 600 oC in an N2/H2 (containing 8% H2) atmosphere for 2 hours with a ramp rate of 5 oC min−1. The final product was designated as WO2.

Synthesis of Ni17W3. 0.4 g NiSO4·6H2O (Macklin, 99.9%) and 0.062 g (NH4)6H2W12O40·xH2O were dissolved in 3 mL DW, followed by stirring until the mixture was completely dissolved. Then, 15 mL of ethylene glycol was added, and the mixture was stirred for another 20 min. Then, 2 mL of NH3·H2O was added dropwise to the above aqueous solution, which was then irradiated in the microwave reactor at 200 oC for 8 min. The precipitate was washed and centrifuged with DW and ethanol before drying. The product was then annealed in an N2/H2 (containing 8% H2) atmosphere at 750 oC for 2 hours with a heating rate of 5 oC min−1 to obtain the Ni17W3 alloy.

Synthesis of Co0.87W0.13–WO2. The Co0.87W0.13–WO2 composite was synthesized via the same in situ phase reconstruction method described for Ni17W3–WO2, with CoC4H6O4·4H2O (Macklin, 99.5%) used as the cobalt precursor in place of NiC4H6O4·4H2O.

Characterizations. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi SU3500) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Titan GC260-300) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) were employed to investigate the surface morphology and elemental distribution of the samples. X-ray diffraction (XRD, LabX XRD-6100, Shimadzu), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM, FEI Tecnai G2 F20), aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-STEM, JEM-ARM300F), and Raman spectroscopy (HR RamLab) were utilized to determine the crystalline structure and phase characteristics of the samples. The surface chemistry of the samples was recorded by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific K-Alpha, Thermo Fisher) using a monochromatic Al Kα X-ray source. The purity of the gas was determined by means of gas chromatographic (GC, GC-7820) analysis.

Electrochemical measurements. Electrochemical tests were conducted in 0.5 M H2SO4 aqueous solution using a CHI 760E workstation and a conventional three-electrode setup. The electrolyte (0.5 M H2SO4) was prepared by diluting concentrated sulfuric acid (XiLONG SCIENTIFIC 98%) with DW, followed by stirring for 30 min. The resulting solution was used immediately after preparation. The Hg/Hg2Cl2 reference electrode (CHI150) was calibrated against a fresh commercial one by measuring their stabilized open-circuit potential (OCP) prior to use. The graphite rod served as the counter electrode. The as-prepared electrocatalysts modified glassy carbon electrode (GCE, CHI104, 3 mm in diameter) served as working electrodes to investigate the HER performance in 100 mL 0.5 M H2SO4. To prepare the modified GCE, 16 mg of electrocatalyst was dispersed in a mixture of 600 μL of DW and 400 μL of N, N-dimethylformamide by ultrasonication to form an ink. Then, 4 μL (0.004 × 16 =0.064 mg catalyst) of the ink was dropped onto a clean GCE and dried (0.914 mg cm−2). Then, the GCE was covered with a Nafion solution (5 wt%, 5 μL). Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was conducted at a scanning rate of 5 mV s−1. Unless otherwise noted, all potentials were compensated for iR corrected and converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) using the Nernst equation: E = E + 0.242 + 0.059 × pH. The pH was measured to be 0.62 ± 0.03 by a pH meter (FE28, Mettler Toledo). The solution resistance was determined by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) performed at an initial potential of −0.22 V vs. RHE in the frequency range of 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz. The Tafel slopes were obtained by plotting the overpotentials (η) vs. log currents (log |j|) derived from the polarization curves. The double-layer capacitance (Cdl) was determined from cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves in the non-Faradic region at scan rates ranging from 1 to 10 mV s−1, which was subsequently used to estimate the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA). By plotting Δj/2 at OCP against scan rates, Cdl is estimated with the slope. Subsequently, ECSA is determined as ECSA = A*Cdl/Cs, where A is the geometric area of the catalyst, and Cs is the specific capacitance (Cs = 0.04 mF cm−2). A Kinetic Isotope Effect (KIE) experiment was performed in 0.5 M D2SO4/D2O electrolyte at a scanning rate of 5 mV s−1. The large current HER properties were obtained using Ni17W3–WO2 modified carbon cloth (Ni17W3–WO2/CC) with a mass loading of 0.914 mg cm−2 as a working electrode. The stability test was conducted using Ni17W3–WO2/CC with a constant current density of 500 mA cm−2. The PEM electrolyzer employed 0.5 M H2SO4 as the electrolyte at room temperature (20 °C) or 80 °C with a scan rate of 5 mV s−1. The catalyst ink for PEM was prepared by dispersing 10 mg of catalyst (IrO₂, Pt/C, or Ni17W3–WO2) in 50 mg of Nafion solution (5 wt%) and 100 mg of ethanol. The mixture was ultrasonicated in an ice bath for 60 min to form a homogeneous suspension. The ink was then brush-coated onto carbon paper and dried under ambient conditions. The catalyst loading was determined by weighing the carbon paper before and after coating and was approximately 10 mg cm−2. A proton exchange membrane (Fumasep FS-990-PK) with a thickness of 90 μm and an area of 2 × 2 cm2 was used as received without pre-treatment. The tungsten blue experiment was performed in a tube furnace at 180 °C for 30 min under a N2/H2 mixed atmosphere (8% H2).

Calculation methods. The DFT calculation was implemented in the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP)67 via the first-principles plane-wave pseudopotential formation and with the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) of Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) function. For the optimization of the structure, a 420.0 eV cutoff energy, 10−5 eV energy convergence accuracy, and 0.03 eV Å−1 residual force, a 1 × 1 × 1 k-mesh is utilized. For the calculation of free energy for adsorbed hydrogen (∆GH*), a 450.0 eV cutoff energy, and 0.02 eV Å−1 residual force are utilized. Adsorption energy (Eads) was calculated as: ∆E = E(surface+H) – E(surface) – 1/2EH2. ∆GH* could be calculated as: ∆GH* = ∆E + ∆(ZPE) – T∆S, where the ∆S represents the entropy change. E(surface + H) refers to the total energy of the system after a hydrogen atom is adsorbed on the basal plane, while E(surface) represents the energy of the clean surface, and EH2 corresponds to the total energy of an isolated H2 molecule. The ∆(ZPE) denotes the zero-point energy (ZPE) difference between an adsorbed hydrogen atom and a gaseous H2 molecule, as determined through normal mode analysis68-69. In this experiment, the entropy of gaseous hydrogen under standard conditions (1 bar of H2, pH = 0, and temperature T = 298.15 K) was taken into account. The strain model was constructed by stretching (1.2% and 0.15%) and compressing (−0.05%) the crystal structure of the model along the direction parallel to the surface. The corresponding models are included in Supplementary Data 1. It should be noted that while DFT calculations provide valuable insights into the electronic structure, there are inherent limitations in modeling the exact material under actual catalytic conditions.

Data availability. The source data generated in this study are provided in the Source Data file. Source data are provided with this paper.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, A non-interfacial H-spillover mechanism is proposed in the Ni17W3–WO2 heterostructure, wherein proton adsorption, migration, and desorption occur entirely within the Ni17W3 phase, bypassing cross-phase diffusion. While the manuscript presents a potentially interesting heterostructured catalyst for hydrogen evolution, the central claim of a "non-interfacial hydrogen spillover" mechanism is insufficiently demonstrated, and several critical mechanistic, theoretical, and benchmarking gaps remain. Therefore, I recommend major revision at this stage, pending substantial improvements in mechanistic clarity.
1. The central claim of a “non-interfacial hydrogen spillover” mechanism lacks clarity and rigorous mechanistic proof. Although DFT simulations show a progression of ΔGH* values across Ni17W3 lattice sites, this does not convincingly exclude interfacial effects. In fact, the presence of a Ni17W3–WO2 heterointerface inherently introduces interfacial contributions. Operando Raman and electrochemical data are insufficient to rule out conventional interfacial H-spillover. The novelty claim must be significantly better substantiated.
2. The authors rely heavily on geometric phase analysis (GPA) to argue for a built-in strain gradient driving proton migration. However, the strain gradient reported (–0.2% to +1.1%) is relatively modest and may not be sufficient to dominate hydrogen diffusion energetics. There is a lack of quantitative correlation between the observed strain and calculated hydrogen adsorption/diffusion energy changes. The direct influence of strain on HER performance must be supported by more rigorous thermodynamic and kinetic models or atomic-resolution strain-mapping.
3. While the authors emphasize that the spillover occurs “entirely within the Ni17W3 phase,” the WO2 phase is still an active part of the heterostructure. The WO2 component contributes >80% by mass (XRD refinement), yet its electrochemical role is limited and primarily described as an electron sink. If WO2 is inactive in H* adsorption and only provides strain/electronic tuning, its inclusion requires more justification, especially as it may reduce the overall electrochemical surface area-to-mass ratio. More rigorous site-specific activity analyses are needed.
4. Although the manuscript compares the overpotential and Tafel slopes against other Ni/W-based systems (e.g., Supplementary Table S1), it fails to adequately benchmark against Pt/C or commercial HER electrocatalysts in acidic media. A side-by-side comparison, including mass activity and durability at industrially relevant current densities, is essential. Additionally, it is unclear whether the catalyst retains stability and activity in a full cell configuration of PEM under a practical operational conditions.
5. The reported Faradaic efficiency of 98.6% (Fig. S14) is not supported by gas chromatography or a precise control experiment to rule out side reactions. Moreover, the exceptionally high stability at 500 mA cm⁻² for 1500 h is striking but post-mortem characterization to confirm catalyst preservation is lacking. Providing comparative degradation profiles and microscopy/XPS data after long-term operation would strengthen the stability claim.
6. The manuscript suffers from several inconsistencies and exaggerated statements. For example, the title and abstract overclaim novelty without clearly defining “non-interfacial spillover” or distinguishing this from conventional intraphase diffusion. Also, some Figures, especially DFT diagrams (e.g., Fig. 5e), are difficult to interpret and should include clearer legends and consistent units.

### Reviewer 2

In this work, the authors report a Ni17W3-WO2 heterostructure designed to enable non-interfacial hydrogen spillover for efficient HER. A strain gradient within the Ni17W3 phase and electron transfer to WO2 are proposed to facilitate hydrogen adsorption, migration, and desorption within the Ni17W3 phase. While the concept of confining hydrogen spillover to a single phase of the heterostructure is intriguing, the manuscript lacks sufficient experimental evidence to substantiate the occurrence of spillover and does not provide a detailed, site-specific mechanistic explanation. Given these unresolved mechanistic ambiguities and the absence of convincing supporting data, the manuscript is not suitable for publication in Nature communications.
1. The synthesis method employed in this study appears nearly identical to that reported for an alkaline HER catalyst (Small 2020, 16, 2005184). The authors should clarify what distinguishes the present system and how these differences enable improved performance under acidic conditions.
2. Non-interfacial hydrogen spillover has been reported previously (e.g., Nat. Commun. 2022, 13, 1189; Small 2025, 21, 2411883), with the latter demonstrating higher HER activity than the present study using non-precious metals. The authors should clarify what advantages the current catalyst provides compared to these previously reported systems.
3. The d-spacing reported in Fig.1h deviates from the known value of the Ni17W3 (111) plane. Moreover, the SAED pattern shown in Fig.1g is insufficiently clear to confirm the crystal planes. More rigorous structural characterization is therefore required to substantiate the phase identification.
4. In the DFT calculations, the hydrogen adsorption energies were evaluated at arbitrary sites without distinguishing between Ni and W atoms in the Ni17W3 phase. To properly elucidate the hydrogen spillover mechanism, the authors should conduct site-specific adsorption analyses to clarify the distinct roles of Ni and W in hydrogen adsorption and migration within the Ni17W3 phase.
5. Experimental validation of the proposed hydrogen spillover mechanism is insufficient. The authors should therefore provide direct evidence of spillover, for example through WO3-based HxWO3 coloration and KIE experiments using D2SO4/D2O.
6. Supplementary Fig.12 reveals evident performance degradation after the 1500-hour durability test, which contradicts the authors' claims of long-term stability. Furthermore, to substantiate the chemical and structural stability of the catalyst, post-durability characterization data (e.g., XPS, XRD, and SEM) should be provided.
7. In Fig.4h, the disappearance of the Ni-O peak suggests H* adsorption at Ni sites. To clarify the spillover pathway, additional in situ Raman measurements at more negative potentials are needed to detect possible M-H vibration peaks as direct evidence of H* accumulation.
8. The manuscript contains several inconsistencies, such as inconsistent peak labeling for identical analytical results and spelling errors in axis labels. A thorough revision is necessary to improve the clarity, consistency, and overall quality of the manuscript.

### Reviewer 3

Review of “Boosting hydrogen evolution reaction via non‐interfacial hydrogen spillover” for Nature Communications.
Recommendation: Major revision
#Comments to the Authors
In this manuscript, the authors report the synthesis of a Ni17W3‐WO2 heterostructure and its application as a non-conventional, non-interfacial hydrogen spillover catalyst for promoting the hydrogen evolution reaction. The study highlights the modulation of hydrogen adsorption and desorption mechanisms by WO2, with Ni17W3 proposed as active sites contributing to enhance HER performance. The conceptual framework is supported by theoretical investigations, and the mechanistic details are elaborated in the manuscript. However, several points require clarification. Therefore, I recommend a major revision of the manuscript to address the following comments.
1. The authors assert that the morphology and particle size of NiWO4 precursor remain unchanged after annealing. However, as evidenced by the high-resolution images of NiWO4 precursor before (Figure S1b) and after annealing (Ni17W3-WO2) (Figure 1c), the morphology is largely similar, but the particle size has increased. Specifically, particle agglomeration has occurred, leading to larger particle sizes. The authors should recognize this observation and update the manuscript accordingly.
2. The amount of evolved hydrogen is reported based on both experimental measurements and theoretical calculations. Additional details regarding the methodology used for the theoretical determination of hydrogen evolution should be provided to ensure clarity and reproducibility. Furthermore, it is observed that the experimental and theoretical hydrogen evolution values at each time interval are remarkably consistent, which is somewhat unusual. The authors are encouraged to include specific numerical values (for both experimental and theoretical results) to facilitate verification and to substantiate the accuracy of the data presented.
3. The hydrogen production rates and Faradaic efficiencies for the individual Ni17W3 and WO2 components should also be calculated. Including these parameters will enable a clearer comparison with the heterostructure and help demonstrate the potential superiority of the interface in enhancing hydrogen evolution activity.
4. The authors have calculated the mass activity of Ni17W3‐WO2 and compared it with that of Ni17W3 and WO2. However, the data points corresponding to the measurement are missing in Figure 3a. The authors should revise this figure carefully to accurately include all relevant data points for proper comparison.
5. In addition to LSV curves of Ni17W3-WO2/CC before and after long-term tests, the structural stability of the catalyst be confirmed through structural (XRD)/morphological (TEM)/elemental analysis before and after long term tests. While the authors mention that the LSV curves after 1500 hours are nearly identical, a slight shift is nonetheless observed. Comment 1: For comment #2, the authors claim that the current work is
advantageous over previous works about non-interfacial hydrogen spillover for its
1

Response 1: Thank you for this critical question, which allows us to clarify and
strengthen the core finding of our work regarding generality. We agree with your
comment that a single material demonstration is insufficient to claim a general design
strategy. Therefore, we have undertaken additional experimental work to explicitly
test the generalizability of our proposed principle.
Our central hypothesis is that the non-interfacial hydrogen spillover mechanism
is enabled by heterointerface-induced strain gradients, not by a specific elemental
composition or a well-defined crystalline structure. To validate this, we designed and
synthesized a distinct Co W -WO heterostructure using the same in situ phase
0.87 0.13 2
reconstruction protocol. The XRD diffraction peaks of the precursor can be fully
indexed to the CoWO phase (JCPDS#72-0479) (Supplementary Fig. 32a). After
4
annealing under a reductive atmosphere (Supplementary Fig. 32b), the diffraction
peaks can be assigned to a face-centered cubic Co W alloy phase (JCPDS#71-7508)
0.87 0.13
and a monoclinic WO phase (JCPDS#32-1393). This new system shares the same
2
design principle but has a different primary alloy composition (Co-W vs. Ni-W).
Remarkably, this Co-W-based heterostructure exhibits the same key mechanistic
signatures as the Ni-W system. To investigate the hydrogen transfer behavior during
the reaction, comparative electrochemical measurements of the Co-W material were
conducted in H SO /H O and D SO /D O electrolytes (Supplementary Fig. 33). A
2 4 2 2 4 2
pronounced kinetic isotope effect (KIE≈2) confirms that the reaction is proton-transfer-
limited, indicative of a spillover process1.
